The company has said that monitoring employees' work performance serves a legitimate interest. Iceland's data protection authority, Persónuvernd, has held that monitoring employees' work performance is permitted only where a specific need justifies it — for example, if supervision cannot reasonably be done by less intrusive means, if the monitoring is required under a collective agreement or a performance-based pay arrangement, or if safety in the area cannot otherwise be assured. In the case cited, the authority found that a restaurant manager's use of security-camera footage to check an employee's work performance did not match the system's stated purpose — security and protecting property — and lacked adequate justification. This decision is relevant to the company's asserted interest, but it speaks more directly to whether the monitoring is necessary and proportionate, and whether it matches its stated purpose. Section II addresses interest legitimacy; necessity and proportionality are addressed separately in Section III. (Persónuvernd, Monitoring of an Employee's Work Performance at a Subway Restaurant, Stjarnan ehf., Case No. 2021051091, decision of 12 March 2024; decision of the Icelandic supervisory authority applying the GDPR and Icelandic electronic-surveillance rules.)
